title: Statistical Arbitrage & Mean Reversion
tagline: Trade relationships, not levels — when two prices that move together drift apart, bet they reconverge.

concept.analogy: Two ferries usually cross a harbor side by side. If one suddenly lags far behind, you don't bet on where the harbor is going — you bet the gap will close, because they're tied to the same tides and routes. Pairs trading is exactly this: you don't predict the market's direction, you predict that a temporarily stretched relationship between two related things will snap back.
paragraphs: Statistical arbitrage ('stat-arb') trades the relationship between instruments rather than their absolute direction. The classic case is pairs trading: find two assets whose prices move together (e.g., two refiners, an ETF and its basket, a stock and its ADR). Form a spread (a combination like A − β·B). When the spread deviates far from its historical mean, go long the cheap leg and short the rich leg, betting the spread mean-reverts.

The key statistical property is cointegration: even if A and B individually wander (are non-stationary), a linear combination of them may be stationary — it has a stable mean and reverts to it. You estimate the hedge ratio β (often via regression), form the spread, standardize it into a z-score, and trade when |z| is large, exiting as it returns toward zero.

This is market-neutral by construction: you're long one leg and short another, so broad market moves largely cancel. Your P&L comes from the spread converging, not from the market going up or down. Risk is that the relationship breaks (the legs decouple permanently — e.g., one company gets acquired) or the spread keeps diverging before it reverts.

In HFT, mean-reversion plays out at very short horizons too: micro-level price moves that overshoot tend to partially revert, and lead-lag relationships (one venue or instrument moving before a related one) create fast, low-risk opportunities — but they decay quickly and are fiercely competed.
points: Trade a spread (A − β·B), not a single price — bet on convergence, not direction.
Cointegration: individual series wander, but a combination is stationary and mean-reverting.
Estimate hedge ratio β, form a z-score of the spread, enter on large |z|, exit near 0.
Market-neutral: broad moves cancel; edge is convergence. Risk: the relationship breaks.
At HFT timescales: micro mean-reversion and lead-lag effects, fiercely competed.
concept.keyIdea: Stat-arb monetizes stable statistical relationships: when a cointegrated spread stretches, bet it reverts. It's market-neutral, so the danger isn't direction — it's the relationship breaking or diverging further before it snaps back.

deepDive.intro: Let's go from 'two prices look similar' to a tradeable, risk-managed signal.

steps.title: Find a relationship
steps.detail: Start from economic logic (same sector, ETF vs. constituents, dual-listed shares, futures vs. spot), then test statistically. Correlation of returns is a weak first filter; cointegration (e.g., Engle-Granger or Johansen tests) is the right tool because it tests whether a combination is stationary, not just co-moving.

steps.title: Estimate the hedge ratio and form the spread
steps.detail: Regress A on B to get β (the hedge ratio): spread = A − β·B. β tells you how many units of B to short per unit of A so the combination is balanced and market-neutral. Re-estimate β periodically — it drifts.

steps.title: Standardize and set entry/exit
steps.detail: Compute the spread's rolling mean and std, then z = (spread − mean)/std. Enter when |z| > z_enter (say 2): if z is high (spread rich), short the spread (short A, long B); if low, long the spread. Exit when z returns toward 0 (or flips). Use a stop (e.g., |z| > z_stop) to cap losses if it keeps diverging.

steps.title: Risk management
steps.detail: Size by volatility and correlation, cap exposure per pair and in aggregate, and detect regime breaks (a structural shift, a merger, an index reconstitution) that invalidate the relationship. The classic failure mode (à la LTCM) is over-leverage plus a relationship that diverges far longer than your capital can withstand.

steps.title: From daily to micro
steps.detail: The same logic compresses to milliseconds: short-term overreactions revert, and a faster-moving leg predicts a slower one (lead-lag). These micro signals are tiny and decay fast, so they reward speed (HFT) far more than the slower, capacity-rich daily stat-arb run by quant funds.

pitfalls: Trading on correlation alone — correlated series can still drift apart forever; test for cointegration.
Treating β as constant — re-estimate; a stale hedge ratio leaves you with directional risk.
No stop / over-leverage — 'the market can stay irrational longer than you can stay solvent.'
Lookahead bias in research — computing the mean/std using future data inflates backtest results (see the backtesting lesson).

interviewQuestions.q: What's the difference between two assets being correlated and being cointegrated, and why does it matter for pairs trading?
a: Correlation measures whether two series' returns move together over short intervals — it can be high even for two series that are slowly drifting apart, and it says nothing about a stable long-run relationship between price levels.

Cointegration means a specific linear combination of the (individually non-stationary) price series is stationary — it has a constant mean and reverts to it. That's exactly what pairs trading needs: a spread that reliably returns to a mean. Trading on correlation alone can leave you holding a spread that wanders off and never reverts; cointegration is the property that justifies betting on convergence.

interviewQuestions.q: Why is a properly hedged pairs trade 'market-neutral', and what risk does that leave you exposed to?
a: If you're long A and short β units of B, and A and B both move with the broad market, the market component of their moves largely cancels in the combined position. So a market-wide rally or selloff has limited effect on the pair's P&L — your exposure is to the *spread* (the relative move), not the market level. That's market-neutrality.

It leaves you exposed to relationship/idiosyncratic risk: the spread diverging further before reverting (timing/drawdown risk), or the relationship breaking permanently (a merger, a fundamental shift, an index change) so the spread never reverts. Also basis/financing and short-borrow costs, and model risk in the hedge ratio. Neutral to the market ≠ riskless.

problems.title: Spread z-score and signal
problems.statement: Given two price series A and B (equal length), a hedge ratio beta, and a lookback window w, compute the current z-score of the spread s_t = A_t − beta*B_t using the trailing-window mean and std (population std, excluding the current point is fine to assume included). Return a signal: −1 (short spread) if z > 2, +1 (long spread) if z < −2, else 0. If std is 0 or fewer than w points exist, return 0.
problems.hint: Compute the spread series, take the last w values, get mean and std, then z = (latest − mean)/std and threshold.
problems.tests: Turning a cointegrated spread into a standardized, tradeable signal.

approach: Form the spread s_t = A_t − β·B_t for all t. Take the trailing window of the last w spread values. Compute their mean and standard deviation.

The z-score of the latest spread is (s_last − mean)/std. A high positive z means the spread is unusually rich → short it (−1); a low negative z means unusually cheap → long it (+1); within the band → no trade. Guard for too-few points or zero variance.

zscore.py
codes.source:
import statistics

def spread_signal(A, B, beta, w):
    n = len(A)
    if n < w:
        return 0
    s = [A[i] - beta * B[i] for i in range(n)]
    window = s[-w:]
    mean = sum(window) / w
    sd = statistics.pstdev(window)
    if sd == 0:
        return 0
    z = (s[-1] - mean) / sd
    if z > 2:
        return -1
    if z < -2:
        return 1
    return 0
